answers: The Tesla Model X that slammed into a highway barrier in California last week and killed the 38-year-old Apple engineer at the wheel had been on autopilot at the time of the crash, Tesla confirms in a blog post. But the company says driver Walter Huang "received several visual and one audible hands-on warning earlier in the drive," adding that "the driver’s hands were not detected on the wheel for six seconds prior to the collision." Tesla also laid some blame on state highway officials, asserting that "the reason this crash was so severe is because the crash attenuator, a highway safety barrier which is designed to reduce the impact into a concrete lane divider, had been crushed in a prior accident without being replaced." The fact that the vehicle was on autopilot is likely to be controversial because, as ABC News notes, driver Huang had reportedly been concerned about it. His brother told KGO that Huang had brought his Model X back to the dealership complaining that when he used the feature, the car kept swerving toward the very same barrier that it eventually struck in the fatal collision. The NTSB is investigating the crash, including the fire that broke out after the collision. The accident follows another in Arizona in which a self-driving Uber struck and killed a pedestrian.

full.prediction:
**Summary of News Passages:**

A fatal crash involving a Tesla Model X occurred on March 23, 2018, on the 101 Highway near Mountain View, California. The 38-year-old driver, Walter Huang, an Apple engineer, died when his vehicle crashed into a barrier that had been previously damaged in an accident and not repaired. The crash took place while the vehicle was on Autopilot, with the adaptive cruise control set to the minimum follow distance. According to Tesla, the driver had received several visual and one audible warning, but his hands were not detected on the wheel for six seconds before the collision. The vehicle logs indicated no action was taken by the driver, contributing to the severity of the crash.

Tesla emphasized that the crash attenuator, a safety barrier designed to reduce impact, had been crushed in a prior accident and was not replaced, leading to the catastrophic damage. The company stated that this level of damage to a Model X had never been seen before. Tesla also highlighted that Autopilot has been shown to reduce crash rates by up to 40% and that vehicles equipped with Autopilot are 3.7 times less likely to be involved in a fatal accident compared to those without it. The company reiterated that while Autopilot does not prevent all accidents, it significantly improves safety for occupants, pedestrians, and cyclists.

Walter Huang's family reported that he had previously complained to the dealership about the vehicle's Autopilot system veering toward the same barrier multiple times. Despite these concerns, the issue could not be replicated at the dealership. His brother, Will, expressed frustration that the barrier was not repaired in time, stating that it could have saved Walter's life. The California Department of Transportation (CalTrans) confirmed that replacement work was scheduled, but delays due to weather could have contributed to the lack of maintenance.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and California Highway Patrol (CHP) are continuing their investigation into the crash. Tesla has not commented on the specific complaints from Walter Huang's family, directing attention to its general safety statistics. The incident has sparked renewed scrutiny of autonomous vehicles, especially following a similar fatal crash involving an Uber autonomous vehicle in Arizona. In response, Arizona's governor suspended Uber's license to test autonomous vehicles on public roads.

Tesla maintains that its Autopilot system is a critical component in making driving safer and that the company is committed to improving safety for all road users. The tragedy has deeply affected Walter Huang's family and friends
